key_terms.meaning: On-state voltage across a conducting power diode; about 0.7 V for a small silicon diode and 1–2 V for a power diode at rated current
Time from the instant diode current crosses zero going negative until it falls back to a small specified value
Area under the negative current spike during recovery; roughly Q_rr ≈ ½ × I_RR × t_rr
Minimum anode current that keeps an SCR on when the gate pulse is removed; I_L is larger than I_H
Minimum anode current below which a conducting SCR turns off
PNPN thyristor drawn as a PNP and an NPN transistor whose collectors feed each other's bases; regeneration starts when α₁ + α₂ → 1
Anode-to-cathode voltage with the gate open at which the SCR turns on by junction avalanche

key_terms.term: Gate trigger current and voltage (I_GT, V_GT)
key_terms.meaning: Smallest gate current and gate voltage that turn on every device of a type at a stated junction temperature
Gate pulse with a fast rise (well under 1 µs) and high initial current, so the SCR turns on quickly over the whole cathode area
A fast rising anode voltage pushes charging current C_j·dv/dt through the junction capacitance, which acts like gate current and can turn the SCR on by mistake
Process of bringing anode current below holding current and holding reverse voltage long enough for the SCR to regain forward blocking
Time for which the circuit keeps reverse voltage across the SCR after current zero; t_c must be greater than the device turn-off time t_q
Turning off an SCR in a DC circuit by an external LC network, an auxiliary SCR or a transistor that forces current to zero
Two SCRs connected in inverse parallel on one chip with one gate; conducts and is triggered in both half cycles of AC
Two-terminal, bidirectional trigger diode that breaks over at about ±30 V and is used to fire a TRIAC
Thyristor that turns off when a large negative gate current pulse (about one-fifth of anode current) is applied
Resistor–capacitor network placed across a device to limit dv/dt, di/dt and absorb turn-off energy
Energy lost per transition because voltage and current overlap; average power P_sw ≈ ½ V_s I_s (t_on + t_off) f_s for linear transitions, where f_s is switching frequency in Hz
Temperature rise per watt of loss, in °C/W, from junction to case to heat sink to ambient
Material number ε·μ·E_c³ that ranks a semiconductor for power work; E_c is critical breakdown field in V/cm

takeaways: A power diode is a switch with a fixed forward drop and a turn-off delay set by reverse recovery, so it matters most at high frequency.
An SCR is a four-layer latch: gate current only starts the regeneration, after which the anode current itself keeps the device on.
A gate trigger circuit must give a fast-rising pulse of adequate current and voltage, not just a slow DC level, otherwise turn-on is local and lossy.
Commutation is the circuit's job, not the device's: you must drop current below I_H and then hold reverse voltage for longer than t_q.
TRIAC and DIAC make a cheap, phase-controlled AC switch, while GTO gives a thyristor-like device that can be turned off from the gate.
Power BJT is current driven, MOSFET is voltage driven with a gate charge, and IGBT puts a MOSFET gate on a BJT output for high-voltage work.
Ratings mean nothing without protection: snubbers limit dv/dt and di/dt, and gate drives must deliver clean, fast pulses with isolated returns.
Switching loss and thermal resistance together decide the heat sink and the maximum switching frequency a design can survive.
SiC and GaN switch faster and block more volts per unit area than silicon, but demand tighter gate drive, careful layout and attention to EMI.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on device structure and characteristics drawn correctly, on numbers with units, and on protection and gate-drive reasoning that follows from those characteristics.

bank.q: Draw and explain the static V-I characteristic of a power diode. Mark V_F, the reverse leakage region and the reverse breakdown voltage, and state typical values for a silicon power diode.
outline: Forward region: exponential rise, then a resistive slope; V_F roughly 1–2 V at rated current
Reverse region: small leakage I_R, often in microamperes to milliamperes
Breakdown at V_BR, never to be reached in normal operation
Why power diodes are made with a lightly doped drift layer: high V_BR but higher V_F

bank.q: Explain the two-transistor model of an SCR and use it to show why the device latches on.
outline: PNPN split into PNP (Q1) and NPN (Q2) with base–collector cross coupling
Anode current I_A = (α₂·I_g + I_leak)/(1 − α₁ − α₂)
Regeneration when α₁ + α₂ approaches 1
Show that once latched, removing the gate does not turn the device off; explain I_L and I_H

bank.q: List the methods of turning on a thyristor and explain each with a small circuit or waveform.
outline: Gate triggering: normal controlled method
Forward voltage (overvoltage) triggering: avalanche, not preferred
dv/dt triggering: charging current through junction capacitance
Thermal triggering: temperature raises leakage until regeneration
Light triggering: used in HVDC valves

bank.q: Compare TRIAC, DIAC and GTO with respect to structure, terminals and typical applications.
outline: TRIAC: inverse-parallel SCRs, one gate, AC phase control in fans and dimmers
DIAC: two terminals, breakover near ±30 V, used to fire a TRIAC
GTO: three terminals, turn-off by negative gate pulse, used in DC drives and traction
Note the poor gate sensitivity of GTO and the half-wave asymmetry of TRIAC

bank.q: A thyristor is to be fired from a control circuit through a pulse transformer. Describe a gate trigger circuit and calculate the gate resistor needed for I_GT = 100 mA at V_g = 1.0 V from a 12 V drive, stating the pulse width and duty.
outline: Series resistor R_g = (V_drive − V_g)/I_GT = (12 − 1)/0.1 = 110 Ω; choose nearest standard value and recheck current
Pulse transformer for isolation; explain volt-second limit and why pulse is short
Pulse width of a few tens of microseconds, duty low to limit average gate power
Fast rise time, and diode or capacitor at gate to sharpen the front

bank.q: Explain natural and forced commutation. For an LC commutation circuit, show how circuit turn-off time t_c is found and state the design condition on t_q.
outline: Natural (line) commutation in AC circuits: current zero comes from the supply
Forced commutation classes: resonant, auxiliary SCR, complementary, pulse, external
C discharges through the SCR giving reverse voltage; t_c = C·V_s / I (for constant-current discharge)
Requirement t_c > t_q with margin; t_q depends on temperature and anode current

bank.q: A power MOSFET switches 300 V, 5 A at 100 kHz. Given t_on = 80 ns and t_off = 120 ns, estimate the switching loss and compare it with the conduction loss for on-state resistance 0.5 Ω and duty 0.5.
outline: Total 21.25 W; switching loss dominates, so reduce f_s or use a faster device
Mention that this estimate assumes linear (triangular) transitions

bank.q: Design a turn-off snubber for a device with rated dv/dt of 200 V/µs, switching 400 V, and carrying 10 A with a stray inductance of 0.2 µH. Choose C and R and justify the component wattage.
outline: C ≥ I·dt/dv = 10 × (1/200) µF = 0.05 µF, take 0.1 µF for margin
R limits discharge current and gives a snubber time constant R·C much smaller than switching period
Snubber loss ≈ ½ C V² f_s, so pick resistor wattage from that
Stray inductance limits di/dt: explain the series inductor or the di/dt rating argument

bank.q: A MOSFET has gate charge Q_g = 60 nC and is driven between 0 and 10 V at 100 kHz. Calculate the gate drive power and explain why a gate resistor of 10 Ω gives a slower turn-on than 2 Ω.
outline: Peak gate current ≈ V/R, so 1 A with 10 Ω and 5 A with 2 Ω
Higher resistance slows charging of C_iss and increases switching loss in the device
Mention Miller plateau and why the gate drive must source and sink current

bank.q: Compare power BJT, power MOSFET and IGBT on drive, conduction drop, switching speed, second breakdown and safe operating area, and say which you would pick for a 400 V, 20 kHz motor drive.
outline: BJT: current driven, low V_CE(sat), slow, narrow SOA with second breakdown
MOSFET: voltage driven, resistive drop I²R, very fast, no second breakdown, best below a few hundred volts
IGBT: MOSFET gate plus BJT output, low drop at high voltage, moderate speed, no second breakdown but has a latching current limit
Justify the IGBT for 400 V, 20 kHz with reasons from the table

bank.q: A thyristor in a DC chopper must turn off in 30 µs while the circuit can hold reverse voltage for only 25 µs. Analyse what happens and discuss two ways to fix the circuit.
outline: t_c < t_q, so the device turns on again when forward voltage returns: commutation failure
Fix by increasing C or the reverse voltage in the commutation circuit to raise t_c
Or reduce switching frequency to give more available time, or use a faster device with smaller t_q
Also check that anode current actually fell below I_H before reverse voltage was applied

bank.q: Evaluate the claim that a silicon carbide MOSFET can replace a silicon IGBT in a 900 V, 50 kHz converter. Discuss benefits and the practical problems.
outline: Higher critical field E_c gives a thinner drift layer and lower on-resistance per unit area
Fast switching with small recovery in the body diode allows higher f_s and smaller filters
Problems: gate drive voltage window, gate oxide reliability, ringing from high dv/dt, EMI, layout inductance
Thermal design changes because the die is small; cost is still higher, so justify by loss saving

bank.q: Two identical SCRs are connected in series to block 2 kV. Explain the problem, propose a solution, and state how you would verify it experimentally.
outline: Leakage currents differ, so voltage splits unevenly; series resistor (static equalising) makes the split nearly equal
RC snubber across each device equalises switching transients
Derate: use two 1.2 kV devices for 2 kV, not two 1 kV devices
Verification: measure voltage across each device with a differential probe at both DC and switching

bank.q: A converter fails in the field with short-circuited devices and excessive junction temperature. Evaluate the combined roles of snubber design, gate drive and heat sink selection in preventing this failure.
outline: Find the root cause path: overvoltage from stray inductance, dv/dt turn-on, or slow gate drive raising switching loss
Snubber reduces peak voltage and dv/dt; correct RC values and short leads
Gate drive: adequate peak current, clean return path, negative bias for fast turn-off
Thermal: junction temperature T_j = T_a + P_total × (R_th,ja); check margin at worst-case ambient
Add fault protection: overcurrent trip, desaturation detection

glossary.def: Branch of electronics that converts and controls electric power using semiconductor switches operating as ON/OFF devices.
Two-terminal P-N junction device built with a thick, lightly doped drift layer so it can block high reverse voltage and carry large forward current.
Delay in turning off a diode because stored minority carriers must be removed before it blocks reverse voltage.
Abrupt end of reverse recovery, which produces a sharp current fall and a large voltage spike; a soft recovery avoids it.
Metal–semiconductor diode with no minority carriers, very fast switching and a low forward drop, but limited reverse voltage.
Four-layer P-N-P-N device that turns on when a gate pulse starts internal regeneration and then stays on until anode current falls below holding current.
The three terminals of an SCR: anode and cathode carry the main current, gate receives the control pulse.
Fraction of emitter current that reaches the collector in a transistor; in the two-transistor model, regeneration needs α₁ + α₂ ≥ 1.
Minimum time the SCR needs, after current zero, with reverse voltage applied, before it can block forward voltage again.
Network of L, C and auxiliary switches that forces the anode current of an SCR to zero in a DC circuit.
Load or self-commutation in which a resonant load current itself creates the zero crossing.
AC power control method in which the firing angle of a thyristor or TRIAC sets the portion of each half cycle delivered to the load.
Four combinations of MT2 and gate polarity in which a TRIAC can be triggered; sensitivity is poorest in the third quadrant.
The anode current above which a GTO can no longer be turned off by its gate.
Graph of permitted device current against voltage for a stated pulse width, inside which the device will not be damaged.
Circuit that converts a control signal into the current or voltage pulse a device gate needs, usually with isolation.
Maximum rate of rise of off-state voltage a device can withstand without turning on by itself.
Maximum rate of rise of on-state current allowed at turn-on, set by how fast the conduction area can spread.
Flat part of the gate voltage waveform during turn-on, where gate charge is used to swing the drain voltage instead of raising V_gs.
Temperature of the semiconductor chip itself; it must stay below the rated maximum, typically 125 °C to 175 °C.
Metal structure that carries heat from the device case to the surrounding air, characterised by its thermal resistance in °C/W.
Material such as silicon carbide or gallium nitride with a band gap well above silicon's 1.1 eV, giving a higher breakdown field.
Field strength at which avalanche breakdown begins; it is roughly ten times higher in SiC than in silicon.
